body.head: Walt Whitman.
body.p: Leaves of Grass. Walt Whitman's poems complete. Philadelphia; Rees Welsh & Co. 12 mo., cloth., 382 pp. Price, $2.

Anything like a review of Walt. Whitman's poems, is impossible in a limited space. Notwithstanding the complimentary notices "the good gray poet" has received from one or two English magazines, and from a few American sources, he is not understood, or else his poems remain, as many have all along thought, a sort of bosh that is made to adhere by an assortment of gluey words. If the Massachusetts censor had kept his opinion to himself that the book was immoral, when it was in the press of James R. Osgood & Co., it is probable that its sale would not have been sufficient to pay expenses. The opinion was not jusitifed, but in deference to it the Osgoods declined to issue the book, and by an arrangement the plates were transferred to the present publishers. Public curiosity having been piqued by the controversy, there has been more demand for the book, and it is not improbable that it will yield a little money yet. For the many who know nothing of how Walt Whitman writes, extracts from this bulky volume, picked out not at random, and yet not with extraordinary labor to select the best, will be made. They represent Walt Whitman, and show the manner of the man's poetic thought. One of his poems commences:

lg.l: Give me the splendid silent sun with all his beams full dazzling,
Give me the juicy autuminalautumnal fruit ripe and red from the orchard,
Give me a field where the unmow'd grass grows
Give me an arbor, give me the trellis'd grape,
Give me fresh corn and wheat, give me serene moving animals teaching content,
Give me nights perfectly quiet as on high plateaus west of the Mississippi, and I looked up at the stars,
Give me odorous at sunrise a garden of beautiful flowers where I can walk undistrub'd,
Give me for marriage a sweet-breath'd woman of whom I should never tire,
Give me a perfect child, give me away aside from the noise of the world a rural domestic life,
Give me to warbie spontaneous songs recluse by myself, for my own ears only,
Give me solitude, give me nature, give me again O nature your primal sanities !

body.p:
And here is one of them entire:
Weave in, weave in, my hardy life,
Weave yet a soldier strong and tall for great campaigns to come,
Weave in red blood, weave sinews in like ropes, the senses, sight weave in,
Weave lasting sure, weave day and night the weft, the warp, incessant weave, tire not
(We know not what the use O life, nor know the aim, the end, nor really aught we know,
But know the work, the need goes on and shall go on, the death-envelop'd march of peace as well as war goes on,)
For great campaigns of peace the same the wiry threads to weave,
We known not why or what, yet weave, forever weave,

Here are two stanzas from a "Song at Sunset":
Splendor offended day floating and filling me,
Hour prophetic, hour resuming the past,
Inflating my throotthroat, you divine average,
You earth and life till the last ray gleams I sing.
Open mouth of my soul uttering gladness,
Eyes of my soul seeing perfection,
Natural life of me faith fullyfaithfully praising things,
Corroborating forever the triumph of things.
